text:
The air in Blackwood Bay had been holding its breath for days, or perhaps it was holding mine. A low, persistent thrum vibrated through the floorboards of my office, a bass note beneath a profound, unnatural quiet. Not the peace of an empty forest, but a silence that felt deliberately enforced, as if some cosmic hand had muted the world beyond my window. Even the old police band radio on my desk, usually a babbling stream of local chatter and static, offered only a whispery, intermittent crackle, like dry leaves scuttling across a tombstone. It was a broken sound, a fractured signal from a world gone strangely inert.

I traced a finger over the worn lines of the Blackwood Bay map tacked to my corkboard, a web of streets and forgotten paths leading to the water's edge. The thrum seemed to rise from the very granite the town clung to, a tremor that settled deep in the bones, not violent, but pervasive. It felt less like the earth shifting and more like the town itself sighing a slow, painful breath. My notes on Eleanor Vance, scrawled alongside obscure historical markers, seemed to pulse faintly in the dim light, illuminated by the sheer weight of the atmosphere.

The unnerving quiet pressed in, heavier now, punctuated by the almost subliminal vibration. It made the mundane details of my investigation — the missing files, the hushed rumors of the lighthouse keeper, the strange bloom of a certain fungi near Miller's Pond — feel suddenly sharper, more urgent. Blackwood Bay wasn't just quiet; it was listening. And whatever it was listening for, it felt like it was about to find it.
